title: the follower never holds the miner's input chain at the same instant (exact tip equality unreachable)
summary: With a steady payment workload the Rust node exceeded the +-2 ordering block window 24 times, peaking 4 blocks behind. Without a workload the same build stayed within 1. Startup is excluded (60 s per process); the post-restart catch-up is NOT, deliberately.
likely_related_to: 2026-09-22-3: every ordering block with transactions falls back to a full BlockTransactions download, so under load the follower pays the download it was supposed to avoid, on top of validating input blocks.
gate: assertions 2 and 3 of the devnet-matrix smoke FAIL on this; 1, 4, 5 and 6 pass.

changes_since_round_1: incremental weak-id index in ergo-mempool (the per-frame full-pool parse is gone)
waitlist_entries raised to 8192 (WaitlistFull no longer fires)
D4 + D5, so reconstruction now succeeds on multi-transaction blocks
round_2_remeasurement.verdict: unchanged: 0 exact matches in 746 same-tip samples. The follower is never WRONG - zero history mismatches, zero digest mismatches, no penalties, heights within 2 - it is simply several input blocks behind a miner publishing roughly one per second.

profile_60s_under_load.tool: perf record -F 199 -g on the release node for 60 s during a funded run

top_costs.reading: bulk copying - body/section buffers and snapshot rebuilds
hashing: transaction ids, weak ids, Merkle roots. Intrinsic to the protocol

the actionable one. drop_in_place<ApiInputBlockEntry> alone is 2.67%, which says the input-blocks REST read-slot snapshot is rebuilt and thrown away far more often than anything reads it. Rebuilding it on change rather than per effect batch is the next thing to try.

profile_60s_under_load.note: the profiled run competed with perf for CPU and produced no multi-tx reconstruction; the numbers are indicative, not a clean measurement

round_3_remeasurement.note: assertions 2 and 3 were restated as consistency-under-lag with hard bounds (p95 <= 8, max <= 16 input blocks). The lag bound is what this finding is now measured against, and it fails by an order of magnitude.

run_a.assertion_6: PASS (20/20 observed in a Rust input block)

run_b.assertion_6: FAIL (0/20 observed in a Rust input block)

round_3_remeasurement.run_to_run_variance: the two runs differ by 2x in lag because the Scala miner's ordering-block acceptance is racy (CandidateGenerator clears cachedCandidate after every accepted input block, so ordering solutions are often rejected). When an ordering block takes minutes instead of ~55 s the input chain under it grows to 180 blocks and a follower with fixed throughput falls proportionally further behind. Lag in INPUT BLOCKS is therefore partly a measure of the miner's stall, not only of the follower.
round_3_remeasurement.escalation: round-3 ruling item 4 parks the single-in-flight validation ceiling (spec 7.4) 'to revisit only if the p95 lag bound fails'. It failed, in both runs, by 10-20x. This is now the blocking item for assertions 2 and 3 and, indirectly, for 5 and 6 under load.

assertion_3_residual.shape: every one is the same: Rust's listed chain still belongs to the PREVIOUS ordering block while `bestOrdering` already names the new one. Not one violation has a Rust block sitting at a different position in Scala's chain - Rust's ids are simply absent from the new chain.
assertion_3_residual.why_the_harness_cannot_key_it_out: on BOTH nodes /blocks/bestInputChain pairs `bestOrdering` (the best HEADER id) with a chain read from the input-block processor - Scala's route does the same (bestHeaderOpt + bestInputBlocksChain()). The two sources are not atomically consistent, and the width of the window is a throughput symptom. Dropping mid-transition pairs (same ordering id as the previous sample, non-empty Scala chain) removes most but not all: the Rust node stays on the old tree for several consecutive samples.
options_for_the_controller: expose the ordering id a chain belongs to on the Rust endpoint, which would make the assertion decidable without guessing
define assertion 3 only over samples where every Rust id is in Scala's chain - which collapses it into assertion 2
accept it as a known artifact and gate on assertion 2's lag bound alone
